title: Michael Sheen campaign on toxic waste sites wins Senedd backing
summary: All parties urge Welsh and UK ministers to ensure polluters pay to clean up contaminated land.
text: Michael Sheen campaign on toxic waste sites wins Senedd backing - BBC News BBC Homepage Skip to content Accessibility Help Your account Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds More menu More menu Search BBC Home News Sport Earth Reel Worklife Travel Culture Future Music TV Weather Sounds Close menu BBC News Menu Home Climate World US & Canada UK Business Tech Science Entertainment & Arts Health More In Pictures BBC Verify Newsbeat Wales Wales Politics Wales Business North West North East Mid South West South East Cymru Local News Michael Sheen campaign on toxic waste sites wins Senedd backing Image source, BBC/Wall to Wall Image caption, Michael Sheen investigated Wales' toxic legacy in a BBC iPlayer documentary By Adrian Browne Wales political reporter Published 30 September 2026 Member of the Senedd from all parties have urged Welsh ministers to work with the UK government to make sure polluters pay for cleaning up contaminated land. A motion introduced by Plaid Cymru MS Niamh Salkeld, backed across party lines, also calls for a UK fund to investigate and remediate sites where costs cannot be recovered, and for a framework to test affected land. The calls come after a BBC documentary by Michael Sheen examined claims toxic waste poisoned people at 14 sites in Wales and England. A Welsh government minister promised a plan to "progressively restore post-industrial land" and protect communities from "potential risks". Earlier this month, Sheen went to Westminster to urge MPs to support a testing programme. Buried with Michael Sheen What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales. Watch on iPlayer In the Senedd on Thursday, one member after another recounted in detail the history of sites in their area that they were worried about. Salkeld, who represents the constituency of Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, said her motion was about "making sure that the legacy of our industrial past is managed properly and fairly". "It's about having a clearer national picture of contaminated land," she said. "It's about prioritising the sites where the risks are greatest. "It's about giving local authorities the support that they need, and it's about making sure that where possible, those responsible for pollution contribute to the cost of putting it right. "The communities living alongside these sites did not create this contamination, so they should not be left with carrying the uncertainty, the potential risks, all the costs." What he told me made my blood run cold - Michael Sheen investigates Wales' toxic legacy Published 11 August Toxic waste sites exposed in Michael Sheen documentary are 'tip of the iceberg' Published 26 August A number of speakers highlighted the results of a Freedom of Information inquiry by the environmental campaign group Friends of the Earth , external , indicating there were potentially over 45,000 contaminated land sites in Wales, with only 82 sites being designated as contaminated. Reform MS Andrew Griffin said communities across Wales living near sites that are potentially unsafe "deserve answers". "They deserve a system capable of establishing the facts, and where action is needed, they deserve to know that the money and the determination are there to see it through. "As their representatives, the least we can do is to make sure their questions are heard and keep asking them until they get a proper answer." Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates highlighted a combined pledge of more than £240m from the previous Welsh government, led by his party, and Labour ministers at Westminster for coal tip remediation. He said this demonstrated "that all levels of government need to act fast and need to act together in partnership" to tackle this pollution. "Councils, citizens and communities cannot afford the cost of remediation, nor can they afford to wait any longer for action." He called on Plaid Cymru ministers to "stand up for the people of Wales by taking urgent action where it can now". Image source, Senedd Cymru Image caption, Niamh Salkeld said a "clearer national picture of contaminated land" is needed Conservative Janet Finch-Saunders said local communities "should be able to understand where these sites are located, what risks have been identified, what action is being taken, and whether that action is satisfactory". "Regular inspections and up-to-date public registers would help," she said. "We must ensure that lessons are learned from previous incidents where contamination occurs, the response should be timely, coordinated, and proportionate, with clear responsibility for investigating the source. "This is not simply about dealing with contamination after it has occurred. It is about prevention, enforcement, and accountability." Rural Resilience and Sustainability Minister Llyr Gruffydd promised the Welsh government was "absolutely committed to developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land and to protect communities from those potential risks that come with that legacy". He said he had heard the "calls for action", pledging he would "ensure that former industrial land is made safe". "I will protect public health and deliver long-overdue environmental justice for the communities that have been most affected by this," he added. The motion was passed with no objections.
